tone_statements.citation: Tang Baiyan 唐柏炎 (record: TANG, Baiyan). 2025. 安順ミャオ語における変調 / A Synchronic Account of Anshun Hmong Tone Sandhi. 千葉大学ユーラシア言語文化論集 = Journal of Chiba University Eurasian Society 27: 121-145 (2025-12-31). Chiba: 千葉大学ユーラシア言語文化論講座. ISSN 2185-7148. doi:10.20776/S21857148-27-P121.
tone_statements.quote: これらの研究によると、ミャオ・ヤオ語の「変調」は大まかに「左側変調」と「右側変調」という2種類にまとめられる。安順ミャオ語は「右側変調」である。つまり、二つの音節が並んだとき、右側の音節は声調が変わるが、左側の音節の声調は変わらないのである。[...] 音韻的には、常に第1声調または第2声調(即ち、ミャオ語祖語のA声調)の音節に後続する音節で起こる。そして、統語的には、語彙レベルや句レベルにしか見られないのであり、句と句の間には確認できていないのである。
tone_statements.translation: According to these studies, 'tone sandhi' in Hmong-Mien languages can broadly be grouped into two types, 'left-side sandhi' and 'right-side sandhi'. Anshun Hmong has 'right-side sandhi': when two syllables stand together, the right-hand syllable changes its tone while the tone of the left-hand syllable does not change. [...] Phonologically, it always occurs in a syllable that follows a syllable in Tone 1 or Tone 2 (i.e. Proto-Hmongic tone A). Syntactically, it is found only at the word and phrase level and has not been observed between phrases.
tone_statements.locator: §1 概説, p.121 (the same passage is reproduced as the [概論] abstract in the Chiba CURATOR record); dialect affiliation statement §2 音韻環境, p.122; sandhi rule list p.122

tone_statements.citation: Castro, Andy and Flaming, Royce and Youliang, Luo (2012). A Phonological and Lexical Comparison of Western Miao Dialects in Honghe. Dallas, Texas: SIL International. 62 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Wang (1983), Xian (2000) and Luo and Yang (2004) identify eight lexical tones for Standard Western Miao, distinguished by initial pitch, final pitch and contour. Breathiness is also a crucial feature of tone in many Western Miao varieties, because two different tone categories sometimes have an identical pitch contour and are then distinguished from each other by the presence or absence of breathiness.11 These eight tones are often denoted by the numbers 1 through 8, and are represented in the SWM orthography by word-final “tone letters”.12 A list of the eight tones, with examples from Standard Western Miao as described by Luo and Yang (2004), is given in Table 4. The specific number of lexical tones in different varieties of Hmong varies somewhat due to tone splits and mergers.
tone_statements.locator: §2.3 'Sketch of Western Miao phonology', pp.8-9, with Table 4 'Tones in Standard Western Miao' (p.9); §5.1.1 'Tones' pp.14-16

tone_statements.citation: Castro, Andy & Gu Chaowen. 2010. Phonological innovation among Hmong dialects of Wenshan. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 3(1): 1-39. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
tone_statements.quote: Both Wang (1983) and Xian (2000) identify eight lexical tones for Standard Western Miao, distinguished by initial pitch, final pitch and contour. Breathiness is also a crucial feature of tone in many Core Farwestern Hmongic varieties, because two different tone categories sometimes have an identical pitch contour yet are distinguished from each other by the presence or absence of breathiness.15 Examples of the same eight lexical tones found in Hmongb Nzhuab, as described by Xiong and Cohen (2005), are given in (4). The specific number of lexical tones in different varieties of Hmong varies somewhat due to tone splits and mergers. The pitch, contour and voice quality of the lexical tones also varies from dialect to dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Mortensen, David. 2004. The development of tone sandhi in Western Hmongic: a new hypothesis. Unpublished manuscript, University of California, Berkeley, 13 March 2004, 11 pp. (formerly online at www.pitt.edu/~drm31/).
tone_statements.quote: The tone sandhi of Hmong Daw (or White Hmong) is by far the best studied aspect of synchronic Hmongic phonology, and it is quite representative of tone sandhi in Hmong dialects. The only significant tonal innovation over PFWHm that these dialects share is the merger of S with C2 (rather than B2, as in A-Hmao). The system is preserved most cleanly in dialects like Dananshan and Dashanjiao (Niederer 1998:87, 108). [...] Xuyong dialect displays a more dramatic innovation: Here C1 and C2 have been remapped to themselves. In essence, the two alternations associated with these tones have disappeared.
tone_statements.locator: §3.3 'Chuanqiandian (Hmong proper)' (immediately before Figure 8; §4 'Discussion and Conclusion' starts on p.8); the ms carries no page numbers
tone_statements.n_tones: 8 categories (A1 A2 B1 B2 C1 C2 D1 D2) plus derived sandhi tone S historically

The system is preserved most cleanly in dialects like Dananshan and Dashanjiao (Niederer 1998:87, 108). sources.note: Reconstructs Proto-Western-Hmongic with four tones A-D already split allophonically into yin/yang registers (A1-D2) and a single ping-triggered (A1/A2) sandhi mapping A2 -> derived sandhi tone S; derives the daughter systems as graphs of remappings/mergers; for Chuanqiandian: S merged with C2, the system 'preserved most cleanly in dialects like Dananshan and Dashanjiao', Xuyong has lost the C1 and C2 alternations (Figure 8 'PWHm ping-driven tone sandhi'); synchronic tone sandhi is thus right-hand, triggered by tones 1/2 in compounds and numeral-classifier constructions.

Breathiness is also a crucial feature of tone in many Western Miao varieties, because two different tone categories sometimes have an identical pitch contour and are then distinguished from each other by the presence or absence of breathiness.11 These eight tones are often denoted by the numbers 1 through 8, and are represented in the SWM orthography by word-final “tone letters”.12 A list of the eight tones, with examples from Standard Western Miao as described by Luo and Yang (2004), is given in Table 4. The specific number of lexical tones in different varieties of Hmong varies somewhat due to tone splits and mergers.
